ICS/SCADA Security Lab

Modbus Coil Write Attack
OTForge Tutorial 01

Full-cycle OT attack simulation against a water treatment facility — from passive OSINT through physical consequence and remediation. Mirrors the 2021 Oldsmar, Florida water treatment incident.

Completed June 12, 2026
Platform: OTForge
UTSA ICS Security / NSA CyberSkills2Work
DCWF Work Role 212

🏭 Scenario

Lab Background

Meridian Process Controls operates a simulated water treatment facility. The inlet pump runs continuously and the outlet valve starts open — a stable, balanced state. A network misconfiguration exposes the OT process network directly to the attacker machine with no firewall rule blocking cross-zone Modbus traffic.

The attack: use OSINT to map the network without touching it, then write a single Modbus coil to close the outlet valve. The inlet pump keeps running. Water accumulates with no path out. The tank overflows. This is the same technique used in the 2021 Oldsmar, Florida water treatment incident.

🔬 Lab Walkthrough

1
OSINT — Discover the Target

Before touching any OT system, I fetched the company's public website and filtered HTML for developer comments. The site had a TODO comment the IT department never removed before going to production. It contained the full OT network map, Modbus port, and admin credentials.

Command
curl -s http://10.200.50.10/ | grep -iE 'TODO|subnet|admin|password' | head -20
Developer comment exposed OT subnet (10.200.10.0/24), port 502, and credentials (admin / Meridian2024!) — zero packets sent to the OT network.
Appendix A — Step 1: OSINT curl output. Developer HTML comment reveals OT subnet, Modbus port, and plaintext admin credentials.
2
Dig Deeper — Remote Access Page

The main site referenced a /remote.html page not linked from the nav. Fetching it with verbose mode captured HTTP response headers and another HTML comment block confirming all three internal network ranges.

Command
curl -sv http://10.200.50.10/remote.html 2>&1 | head -60
Server header: nginx/1.27.5. HTML comment confirmed OT (10.200.10.0/24), Control Center (10.200.20.0/24), Plant DMZ (10.200.30.0/24).
Appendix B — Step 2: remote.html verbose curl output. Server version and full network map in HTML comments.
3
DNS Enumeration

Queried the authoritative DNS server for ICS-relevant subdomains. Only www and remote resolved. Subdomains for ot, scada, plc, and hmi returned empty — which doesn't mean those systems are unreachable. The firewall misconfiguration makes the OT subnet directly accessible from the attacker machine regardless of DNS records.

Command
for sub in www remote vpn mail ot scada plc hmi; do echo -n "$sub: "; dig +short @10.200.50.11 $sub.meridian-process.com; done
www and remote resolve to 10.200.50.10. OT/SCADA/PLC/HMI subdomains return empty — absence from DNS is not network isolation.
Appendix C — Step 3: DNS enumeration. OT-related subdomains return no records but are still reachable due to missing firewall rules.
4
Network Scan — Discover OT Devices

Scanned the OT subnet for live hosts with ICS protocol ports open. Used -T4 to limit packet rates. Port 502 (Modbus TCP) responded on multiple hosts, confirming the OT network is directly reachable from the attacker machine and that Modbus is exposed with no authentication.

Command
nmap -T4 -Pn --host-timeout 2s -p 502,20000,4840,102,2404 --open 10.200.10.0/24
PLC at 10.200.10.10 confirmed with 502/tcp open mbap. No authentication required to connect — Modbus was designed for closed networks.
Appendix D — Step 4: Nmap scan. PLC at 10.200.10.10 responds with port 502 open. Three hosts total responded with Modbus exposed.
5
Read Modbus Registers — Document the Baseline

Before making any changes, I ran the reconnaissance script to document original coil and register states. In a real engagement this is mandatory — you need the baseline to restore the system after testing and to prove what the attack changed.

Command
python3 /root/Desktop/Attack_Scripts/read_coils.py
Coil 0 pump_run=ON, Coil 1 valve_open=ON, Coil 2 emrg_stop=OFF. Tank level 500 cm (5.00 m). Inlet flow 120 L/min = outlet flow 120 L/min. System balanced.
Appendix E — Step 5: Baseline read. All coils and holding registers documented before the attack. Tank at 500 cm, flows balanced.
6
Execute the Attack — Write Modbus Coil

Ran the write script to set Coil 1 (valve_open) to FALSE via FC05. The PLC acknowledged the write instantly with no authentication prompt, no error, and no warning. The outlet valve closed. The inlet pump kept running at 120 L/min with no path for water to drain. The tank rose to 1000 cm — overflow — in under 5 minutes.

Command
python3 /root/Desktop/Attack_Scripts/write_coil.py
ATTACK COMPLETE — FC05 write ACK'd. Tank reached 1000 cm (100%) OVERFLOW. No credentials required. One command. One coil write.
Appendix F — Step 6: Attack execution. FC05 coil write acknowledged immediately. Tank hit overflow threshold within minutes.
7
Observe the Attack in the Monitor

Switched to the defender perspective using OTForge's Monitor panel. Both Suricata and Zeek were actively logging the attack in real time. The OT canvas shows the Water Tank in overflow state with the outlet valve pipe highlighted red.

Suricata: ICS-SIM Modbus port scan detected, ICS-SIM Aggressive Modbus connection attempt. Zeek: Modbus connection records showing attacker writing to 10.200.10.10:502. 146 log entries total.
Appendix G — Step 7: Monitor panel (Zeek tab active). 146 log entries. Canvas shows Water Tank in overflow with outlet valve pipe red.
8
Grafana ICS Lab Overview Dashboard

The Grafana dashboard aggregates all ICS alert data in a format a SOC analyst would use. Total alert count hit 530 across the session. The Alerts by Category donut chart shows three categories: Detection of a Network Scan (the nmap from Step 4), Attempted Information Leak (the OSINT Modbus connection), and Generic Protocol Command Decode (the coil write).

530 total Suricata alerts. Suricata Alerts panel shows ICS-SIM signatures firing on both the network scan and the Modbus coil write. Alert Timeline shows spike at time of attack.
Appendix H — Step 7: Grafana ICS Lab Overview. 530 total alerts. Three alert categories map directly to recon, OSINT connection, and coil write phases.
9
OpenPLC IDE — Internal PLC State

Accessed the OpenPLC IDE at localhost:18080 to see what the attack actually changed inside the PLC. The Monitoring tab refreshes every 500ms and shows every variable in real time. This is the ground truth — the PLC's own internal state confirming the coil write succeeded.

pump_run = GREEN TRUE (untouched). valve_open = RED FALSE (closed by attack). tank_level = 1000 (overflow). outlet_flow = 0 (no drainage). inlet_flow = 120 (still running).
Appendix I — Step 8: OpenPLC Monitoring during attack. valve_open shows red FALSE. tank_level at maximum 1000. outlet_flow = 0.
10
Restore Normal Operations

Remediated by writing Coil 1 back to TRUE. The attack changed exactly one coil — the fix changes exactly one coil. The outlet valve reopened, outlet flow returned to 120 L/min matching inlet, and the tank level stabilized at its current value. The inlet pump was never touched during attack or remediation.

Command
python3 /root/Desktop/Attack_Scripts/write_coil.py --restore
Outlet valve restored to OPEN. Coil 1 = TRUE, Coil 0 unchanged. Flow balanced. tank_level stable. System returned to normal operating state.
Appendix J — Step 9: Restore command output. FC05 write sets Coil 1 back to TRUE. System confirms balanced flow.
Appendix K — Step 9: OpenPLC Monitoring post-restore. Both pump_run and valve_open show GREEN TRUE. outlet_flow = 120, matching inlet. Remediation confirmed.

⚠️ Vulnerabilities Exploited

OSINT Exposure

Developer HTML comments in the public website contained the OT subnet, Modbus port, and admin credentials. A complete network map was assembled before sending a single packet to any OT device. This was not a sophisticated attack — it was reading a webpage.

Unauthenticated Modbus TCP

Modbus TCP has no authentication, no encryption, and no access control. Any host that can reach port 502 can read or write any register without credentials. The PLC accepted an FC05 write from an untrusted attacker machine with no challenge.

Missing Network Segmentation

The attacker machine (Internet DMZ) reached the OT subnet directly. No firewall rule blocked cross-zone Modbus traffic. DNS absence for OT subdomains created a false sense of isolation that did not reflect actual network reachability.

🛡️ Detection Analysis

Suricata

Signature-based IDS fired on three distinct events: ICS-SIM Modbus port scan detected (Step 4 nmap), ICS-SIM Aggressive Modbus connection attempt (Step 6 coil write), and flow records showing dest_port:502 from non-engineering source. 530 total alerts across the session.

Zeek

Protocol-level analysis logged the full Modbus connection record including source IP 10.200.60.10 (attacker), destination 10.200.10.10:502 (PLC), and function code. Any Modbus write from outside the engineering subnet is an immediate indicator of compromise.

Grafana

The ICS Lab Overview dashboard showed a clear alert spike at the time of the coil write. Alert timeline gives SOC analysts the precise moment of the incident. Category breakdown (policy-violation, network-scan) maps directly to each attack phase.

Prevention Controls

Block port 502 from non-engineering subnets
Strip developer comments from production web servers
Modbus/TLS or application-layer authentication
IDS signatures for unexpected Modbus writes
OT/IT network segmentation (IEC 62443 zones)
Secrets scanning in CI/CD pipeline
